summary.text: An 83-year-old female with a history of congenital diaphragmatic hernia and osteoporosis presented to the emergency department in January 2024 with coffee ground vomiting twice and generalized abdominal tenderness. On arrival she was hypotensive, hypoxic and tachycardic. After stabilization, chest X-ray and CTA were performed, leading to admission under general medicine.

Imaging showed a diaphragmatic hernia containing bowel, a large hiatal hernia involving the stomach and large bowel, and a filling defect in the right main pulmonary artery indicative of pulmonary embolism, with pleural effusion and compressive atelectasis. White blood cell count was increased with left shift and blood and urine cultures were negative. Bedside OGD showed a large paraesophageal hernia with multiple ulcerations but no active bleeding.

She received antibiotics, oxygen, a nasogastric tube that drained coffee ground vomitus and an omeprazole infusion, while pulmonology advised against anticoagulation until bleeding ceased. Ten days later she had desaturation and decreased consciousness, and two weeks after admission she was confused and progressed to respiratory failure. She improved with laxatives. A subsequent chest CT showed effusions, and low-dose loop diuretics were started.

She was eventually stabilized, and chest X-ray was repeated upon discharge. She was discharged in good condition without a nasogastric tube, with laxatives prescribed and relatives instructed on a diet avoiding gas-inducing or constipating foods. Her comorbidities made her unfit for laparoscopic repair, so conservative treatment was used.

article_limitations: Visual status of figures in this annotation stays not_inspected; actual pixels are reviewed in visual.json.
Oxygen support at discharge conflicts between the case text (98% on room air) and the conclusions (discharge with supplemental oxygen); both carrier facts are review_only.
Table 1 (ABG) takes its time (two weeks after admission) from the sentence that names the ABG; the PO2 reference range is printed as 75-11 mmHg; the nasogastric drainage volume is printed as "2 lL".
Whether the Ten days later deterioration and the two-weeks-after-admission respiratory failure are the same episode is not stated; they have different anchors and no order is asserted between them.
The result of the planned Doppler ultrasound and any later anticoagulation are not reported; the Type IV classification appears only in the abstract.
Discussion statements about mechanisms (chronic pressure, blood stasis) and surgical repair with literature citations are interpretation or general background and are not recorded as facts.
